summary:
Quebec is a province of Canada and stands under Canada's national framework: federal criminal law and the federal human-rights regime apply in Quebec as in every other province. Provincially, the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms has prohibited discrimination because of gender identity and gender expression since 2016, reaching employment, housing, and public and private accommodation.

Enforcement through the province's own machinery is documented. On 10 June 2024 the Quebec Human Rights Tribunal found that a Montreal bar had discriminated against a trans woman in hiring because of her gender identity, ordering the employer to pay $10,000 in moral damages, $4,000 in punitive damages and $118.40 for unpaid training. That is the most recent tribunal decision documented in this record.

Quebec's rules on sex designation and identity documents were reshaped by litigation. After a two-month trial at which 29 witnesses testified, the Quebec Superior Court declared provisions of the Civil Code of Quebec invalid because they violated the fundamental rights of trans, intersex and non-binary people (2021 QCCS 191). The Quebec Court of Appeal largely upheld the decision (2024 QCCA 348), and the ruling led to legislative reform of the Civil Code.

Correctional placement has moved in the opposite direction. On 19 June 2025 Quebec's public security minister announced that transgender inmates in the province will be incarcerated according to their anatomical sex rather than their gender identity, citing fairness and safety as the priorities. The directive was issued just after a trans woman convicted of murdering her partner and children sought a transfer to a women's prison. Advocates stated that the policy violates the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms. It replaced the province's previous practice of considering gender identity in correctional placement.

On family status, a 2002 amendment to the Civil Code of Quebec created civil unions giving couples, regardless of gender or sexual orientation, the same effects as marriage in matters of family direction, parental authority, expenses, family residence, family patrimony and compensatory allowance. The status is valid only in Quebec.
tangentialFactors:
Statistics Canada published police-reported hate crime data for 2024 on 30 March 2026: 4,882 hate crimes were reported nationally, 1% above 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000, which fell 2% in 2024 and rose 142% since 2018. Provincial rates ranged from 5.3 per 100,000 in Manitoba and Newfoundland and Labrador to 16.0 per 100,000 in Ontario, with eight provinces stable or declining. The release windows carry no Quebec-specific rate, so this source does not place Quebec above or below the national figure.

The underlying analysis of that national data was produced by Egale Canada, an LGBTIQ+ organisation, and covers sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations in the police-reported figures.
localsOnly:
Discrimination complaints on the grounds of gender identity and gender expression run under the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms and are heard by the Quebec Human Rights Tribunal, which has awarded damages against an employer on precisely that ground, in the 10 June 2024 decision above.

2021 census data cited by Éducaloi puts transgender people at 0.14% of Quebecers aged 15 and older, and 0.27% of those aged 15 to 34.

The correctional placement directive of 19 June 2025 governs where transgender people in Quebec serve custodial sentences, and by its terms applies to them as residents of the province's own prison system.

Quebec legalised same-sex adoption in 2002, and its civil union status, created the same year, is recognised only within Quebec.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Quebec-specific hate-crime rate appears in the Statistics Canada release windows reviewed here, so whether Quebec sits above or below the national 12.1 per 100,000 is unresolved in this record. The national figures are raw counts as well as rates, and the provincial ordering by count would track population.

Whether the correctional placement directive announced on 19 June 2025 has been challenged in court, suspended, or since amended is not sourced. The record documents the directive and the advocates' position that it breaches the Quebec Charter, and nothing further on its legal status.

The scope, date and content of the Civil Code reform that followed the Centre for Gender Advocacy ruling are not set out in the sources. What the current rules for changing sex designation on Quebec identity documents and civil status records now require is unresolved here, as is any entry-document or screening consequence for a visitor.

The Egale Canada report cited alongside the Statistics Canada release is a national analysis; no Quebec breakdown from it is sourced.
